items.content:
Andrii and the SOC Prime team have just launched LogTotal and I find the concept quite interesting

You can upload a collection of security logs, run detection rules against the events, correlate the matches into potential attack chains, and use AI to help interpret the results.
What I particularly like is the architecture. Instead of throwing millions of log events at an LLM, it starts with detection rules and correlation, using AI later in the process to help investigate and explain the findings.

Another interesting detail is the approach to privacy. Sensitive identifiers can be pseudonymized locally before uploading the logs. The sanitizer is even available as open source, with a CLI that can run completely offline. So if you don't want to rely on JavaScript delivered by a website, you can inspect the code and sanitize your logs in your own environment before uploading.

Sanitizer: https://t.co/VpMx44CZC7

I think that's a sensible direction for AI-assisted security investigations. It also makes retrospective log analysis accessible without having to set up an entire SIEM infrastructure.

I haven't tested it myself yet, and I'd be more interested in the quality of the detections and correlations than the advertised rule count or processing speed.

But the approach makes sense to me. Definitely worth a closer look.

items.content:
This @BeyondTrust incident is worth reading, especially if you work in detection engineering or threat hunting.

@Mandiant says ARMORY CASTLE exploited CVE-2026-102764 in BeyondTrust Remote Support as a zero-day.

Post-exploitation got ugly:

- SAWFLY PHP webshell
- Service account -> root
- Attempted credential vault extraction
- Persistent passwordless root access
- Systematic log deletion
- BARECLAW WebSocket/SOCKS5 tunneler
- Admin session abuse
- Pivoting into downstream systems

But the part defenders should read twice:

BeyondTrust says its sensors fired high-severity alerts in real time when the actor escalated privileges.

A third-party automated triage system closed them as false positives.

Their separate threat-intelligence-driven hunting pipeline later surfaced the activity.

That is such an important detection engineering lesson.

Having telemetry and alerts is only part of the job. You still need strong detection engineering, active threat hunting, validation, R&D and people who understand what the adversary is actually doing.

The sensors saw it. The surrounding detection process failed to escalate it.

Excellent research and transparency from the @Mandiant and @BeyondTrust teams.

items.content:
> We now have very sophisticated and relatively cheap tools that allow you to magically rewrite all software to be more secure. You can find all the bugs, write code that is secure by default, and use models to defend everything

few random thoughts, i am not sure i agree with this. writing more code is generally a bad idea, for a few reasons. i think you need to design systems by reducing the amount of code whose correctness is security critical not by writing more, and build strong isolation boundaries.

take v8, for instance. can we rewrite the entire engine to be secure by default and eliminate all the jit bugs? the level of intelligence required to do that seems far beyond what current models are capable of.

second, you are rewriting complex software using a model that will be obsolete in a few months. the code it produces will remain, and you are back to the same problem  of vulnerabilities when more intelligent model comes up.

i think software complexity massively expands the vulnerability search space. there is no reason to believe you can exhaustively find all bugs by throwing more intelligence or tokens at it. unless you can formally verify the relevant properties, how do you even establish that the software is secure?

i do agree that rewriting c code in memory safe languages like rust can eliminate entire classes of vulnerabilities. for instance, porting image parsers to rust could kill a lot of memory corruption bugs. but you still have logical bugs, and memory safety alone doesn’t make software secure.

items.content:
i don't think this favors defenders for now. there are just so many latent bugs out there that the asymmetry is heavily skewed towards attackers. you can pop pretty much any company in a few days. it's not even that hard anymore, and you can do irreparable damage in that time.

i also don't think putting models behind cyber guardrails stops any determined adversary. it's just friction, they can do the same with open models. something that takes 2 days might take a week instead, thats all there is.

my bet is on money. just follow the money, pretty much everywhere. there are way more humans incentivized to do bad things for money than for some nation state objective, ideology, or just fun. look at call center scams, it's literally an industry.

now, hacking a company, dumping its source code or IP, and actually figuring out how to monetize that is complicated. there's a lot of friction between compromising something and making money from it.

OTOH, consider crypto. find a bug in an on-chain protocol or smart contract, exploit it, take the money, and launder it through privacy protocols. the path from exploit to profit is much shorter.

or take cryptominers. if you have an exposed VM running vulnerable software, there's a decent chance someone's already mining on it. just look at the spam in your Apache logs. people have been spraying and praying with automated exploits long before AI.

and now consider LLM tokens. the METR incident where an attacker exhausted $700k worth of tokens is good example, i am sure many other companies tokens being exhausted magically. i'm sure those VMs had other potentially valuable data, but the attacker went after tokens. why? think about it.

items.content:
RT @cr3ghost: This is why the anti-cheat arms race is getting so interesting.

Riot is pushing Vanguard further into hardware-backed trust, attestation, VBS/HVCI, IOMMU and deeper platform security.

At the same time, AI-assisted reverse engineering is making it much faster to tear apart the software sitting on top of those protections.

@k0mkc is showing heavily devirtualized VGK internals and says he can now devirtualize the entire thing.

On the EAC side, @in19h has published tooling that recovers large parts of a heavily virtualized Easy Anti-Cheat Linux sample into readable code and IDA artifacts:

https://t.co/gp1E7W4Uon

There is an important parallel here with EDR.

An EDR is only as effective as the detection engineering, threat hunting and R&D behind it. Anti-cheat works the same way.

You need researchers constantly following new techniques, detection engineers turning that research into useful telemetry and detections, and people actively hunting for behaviour that existing rules may miss.

That means continuously keeping up with:

- new cheat architectures
- kernel abuse
- BYOVD
- hypervisors
- DMA
- firmware tricks
- input manipulation
- virtualization + obfuscation
- new bypass techniques

The game was already there. AI is speeding it up and lowering the barrier to reversing, classification, devirtualization and research.

That forces both sides to iterate faster.

A lot of respect to the Vanguard team as well. They have clearly been keeping up with some of the most cutting-edge work in Windows security, hardware-backed trust, kernel security and anti-cheat research, and their recent Vanguard On-Demand changes show how quickly the defensive side is evolving too.

This is becoming a much faster research cycle on both sides.

Where does the arms race go next?

Huge credit to @k0mkc and @in19h for the research.

items.content:
RT @chux13786509: 🔴 RED TEAM OPSEC BREAKDOWN

A new report from Mandiant details how ARMORY CASTLE (UNC5221) exploited a BeyondTrust Remote Support 0day to gain access and manage cyber operations.

The TTPs reveals OPSEC failures worth examining 👇

1️⃣ Log deletion didn't erase the evidence

UNC5221 used 'rm -f', which is a gift for DFIR teams.

2️⃣ Persistence left forensic artifacts

The actor created zz-root-persist, a startup script that modified /ns/config/sudoers.template to grant a service account passwordless sudo, then invoked bt-sysconfig to apply the change.

3️⃣ A disguised SUID backdoor

ARMORY CASTLE copied /bin/sh to /usr/bin/dbus-authd, changed its ownership to root, and enabled the SUID bit.

Despite the legitimate looking filename, the binary's origin, ownership, and permissions provided concrete hunting opportunities.
This is maybe the most common technique to preserve privileged access, and definitely the first thing to look for when hunting backdoors on a Linux server. 

4️⃣ The custom tunneler created detection opportunities

The BARECLAW SOCKS5 tunneler listened on 127.0.0.1:19800. The actor modified HAProxy configuration to expose it through the custom URI path /uidchanarge.

The tool also used WebSockets and obfuscation, while TLS was not enabled in the observed deployment.

5️⃣ Privilege changes generated audit events

Using compromised administrator credentials, the actor raised Jump Item and team permissions from No Access to Administrator, generating user_changed events.

🔥 The takeaway: Seems like even sophisticated tooling and deliberate anti-forensics don't guarantee good OPSEC.
Even though UNC5221 had a powerful 0day in their hand, they lost it for being sloppy.
